title: Creation
tomorrow: why would captives pray for the city that conquered them?

cards: The compost bin by the back door smells about how it sounds, and somebody still has to decide it's worth it. Job has a far bigger question.
He has lost nearly everything, and chapter after chapter he has demanded that God explain himself. Then, the book says, “the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind.” Finally.
And the answer opens with a question of its own: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?”

teach.h: A TOUR OF SNOW, SEA AND GOATS.
teach.b: Then God takes Job on a tour. The sea, shut in behind its doors. The storehouses of the snow.
Wild goats giving birth where nobody watches. An ostrich, a war horse, a hawk.
And rain, sent “on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, wherein there is no man.” That's the surprise inside the answer. God waters land nobody lives on, for no human reason at all.
The tour never explains Job's suffering. What it does is make the world bigger than Job, and bigger than any of us.
Psalm twenty-four says the same thing in one line: “The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.” Not ours, then. His, and lent.

teach.h: VERY GOOD, BEFORE ANYONE USED IT.
teach.b: Genesis has God look at what he made and call it “very good” before anyone is around to use it.

Some Christians start their care for creation right here: the earth isn't ours to use up; it's borrowed, and borrowed things get handled with care. Cutting one kind of waste is a small way of saying so.

how: Some churches keep a season of prayer for creation, bless gardens, fields and animals, or run recycling and food-waste projects; the Psalms and Job are prayed as words of wonder at the world.

games.q: your family's yard sale ends with a pile nobody bought. the easy move is the dumpster. what does Job's rain on empty land suggest?
o: things have worth beyond your use, so find them a next home.
if nobody bought it, it has no value left to protect.
God owns the earth, so what you throw out isn't your concern.
games.why: God waters land where no man is: creation has worth beyond human use. borrowed things deserve a next home.

practice: Look around and find one thing about to be thrown away: a jar, a bag, the end of a loaf, a sheet printed on one side. Hold it through the sit and decide its next use, then set it where that use can happen.
If you pray, you can say the psalm's line over it: the earth is the LORD's.
